newsitem.title: USA: Dow seen weaker as blue chips take a breather.
newsitem.headline: Dow seen weaker as blue chips take a breather.

text.p: After its worst shellacking in 4-1/2 months on Tuesday, the Dow industrials will likely retreat further early Wednesday as the market catches its breath from its record-shattering run.
S&P 500 futures "portend a down 30 opening for the Dow, barring unforeseen circumstances," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
The Dow shed 79 points or 1.21 percent to 6443 Tuesday, its biggest point loss since July 15's 161-point tumble. But small and mid caps fared better and may continue to outperform.
Analysts could not pinpoint a reason for the late waves of program selling that sent the Dow skidding from down 50 to down 80 points in the last 10 minutes of trading Tuesday.

But they noted blue chips were due for a pause after rallying some 500 points or eight percent in November amid euphoria over a still-politically divided Washington, lower interest rates and signs the economy is growing at a more sustainable pace.
"What you saw was more of a blow-off. Stocks have done very well in terms of the Dow and market breadth was quite good," said Richard Cripps of Legg Mason Wood Walker.

Cripps, Legg Mason's chief market strategist, sees early weakness Wednesday and then bargain-hunting amid small- and mid-cap stocks, which have lagged the Dow's ferocious rebound from the July selloff.

He noted that large cap blue chips such as General Electric Co, off four to 99-1/4, and Procter & Gamble Co, off 3-7/8 to 104-3/4, were being punished as the dollar has strengthened recently. Investors fearful of the negative impact of a stronger dollar on a multinational corporation's overseas earnings would likely seek solace in smaller cap names, Cripps said.
Another support for smaller caps is the so-called January effect when small stocks typically outperform large caps.

Bleier noted "about a dozen little stocks are up 20-30 percent over the last few days. Yes, the market is broadening out (which is generally healthy for the overall market) but there is speculation in the smallest, most laggard stocks. Sometimes that lasts a long time and sometimes it's the bell that signals profit-taking. Now it signals the latter."
"The market is a herd beast. It was pure emotion on the way up and will be on the way down," he said, noting a virtual absence of sellers over the recent past.
Philip Rettew, a technical analyst at Merrill Lynch, saw "some decline" with "more apparent weakness in blue chips than secondaries and then we'll get in gear for another move up."
He said the Dow's near-term support was way down at 5200, although he was not calling for a test of the level.
"We could go down 100-200 points and then go back up again. A lot of damage could be done in the Dow with just a few stocks," Rettew said.
Like other analysts, Rettew noted that the Dow's 79-point loss Tuesday, while the largest seen for a while, "is not a big deal percentage-wise" at 1.21 percent.
"We just need a breather in here someplace," he added. "It's a rest, but for an ongoing bull market."
But Paul Rabbitt, a quantitative analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, also remains optimistic about the market's near-term prospects.
Mutual fund "inflows are seasonally starting to pick up with year-end charitable trust endowments and bonuses. There's a lot of liquidity generated and a certain amount flows to stocks," he said.
"I'm impressed by the breadth. We're not in the latter stage of a bull market. The trend is still up and inflation is low."
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721
